title: Benchmark methodology workshop \u0014 runtime & VPC deep dive
topics: KV cache warmup and hit-rate measurement
summary: Workshop focused on designing an apples-to-apples benchmark for BrightScale's conversational agents. Covered prompt set curation, load generation patterns, KV cache warmup, batching and quantization impacts, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed to run pilot harness on Redwood Dedicated and provide tooling and config templates.
next_steps: Redwood to share benchmark harness repo (locust + runner) and example configs
BrightScale to provide sample prompts and 24-hour production trace for load pattern
SE to propose quantization profiles and expected regressions matrix

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-20
Start: 09:15 UTC
Duration: ~82 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen, Mateo Ruiz (Redwood); Priya Nair, Omar Haddad, Sinead O'Connor (BrightScale)

[00:00] Ava Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick housekeeping, i'll drop the slide deck and the benchmark template in the chat after  but Mateo's going to run through the methodology and we'll dig into your questions about VPC and on-prem constraints.

[00:18] Priya Nair: Sounds good. Our main goals are making sure any benchmark we run is representative of our prod workload, and that the comparisons between quantized vs fp32 and hosted vs dedicated are apples-to-apples. We had some weird results last time where latency improved but quality dipped.

[00:33] Mateo Ruiz: Totally understood. high level plan: curate prompt sets by traffic percentile, replay arrival traces to reproduce concurrency shape, warmup KV cache systematically, measure p50/p95/p99 latency and throughput, then sweep batching and quantization. we'll also control for context length, tokenizer differences, and seeding to reduce variance.

[00:53] Sinead O'Connor: quick question  when you say warmup KV cache, are you pre-populating with full session histories or just prefixes? Cause our sessions are long and we rely heavily on prefix caching.

[01:03] Mateo Ruiz: Good call. we recommend two warmup strategies: 1) full session replay where you push the exact previous tokens into the cache, 2) prefix-warmup where you only replay a fixed prefix length representative of your 90th percentile. We'll measure hit rate by token and by request. Note that K V cache (transcription sometimes: "K V") hit-rate can look artificially high if the workload has a lot of repeated system prompts.

[01:30] Omar Haddad: On the load side, we have a mix: short queries from our search widget and long multi-turn conversation flows. How do you recommend mixing these in load generation?

[01:40] Mateo Ruiz: Two approaches: mixed-synthetic (sample from your distribution and generate a mix proportionally) or trace-replay (exact production arrivals). For latency-sensitive SLOs we prefer trace-replay because it preserves inter-arrival bursts and cold start patterns. For scalability stress tests, a randomized mix is fine. Also important: model-side batching behavior depends on QPS spikes vs steady-state QPS.

[02:05] Priya Nair: Regarding quantization — we ran an int4 experiment and saw a 5% drop in Rouge-L on one eval set. Is that typical?

[02:12] Mateo Ruiz: Some drop is expected. our advice: run a regression matrix across representative prompt sets, not just a single eval. measure both semantic metrics and prompt-specific criteria (e.g., instruction-following, hallucination rate). Also consider mixed precision: keep attention/key computations at higher precision and quantize feed-forward layers. We'll share quant profiles that tend to preserve quality.

[02:40] Speaker 1: (mumbled) also watch out for tokenization-induced length changes — sometimes quantized runtimes add special tokens or modify whitespace handling, which changes cost per request.

[02:55] Sinead O'Connor: On the security / VPC side, our compliance team needs clarity on egress paths and audit logs. If we run Dedicated in our VPC, how do we capture per-request telemetry and maintain KMS keys?

[03:10] Ava Chen: For Redwood Private / Dedicated in VPC we can integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key management, and we stream audit logs to your log sink (s3/bigquery/splunk). We'll send the SOC2 and ISO docs; Mateo will include the exact fields we surface in request-level telemetry.

[03:32] Omar Haddad: Network impact — we're worried about an extra 10-30ms egress overhead to the model nodes in another AZ. Does that skew latency numbers in your benchmarks?

[03:40] Mateo Ruiz: It can. two ways to handle: 1) measure network-only baseline (ping/TCP handshake + TLS) then subtract from model round-trip to isolate inference time, or 2) run the benchmark inside the same AZ/VPC and record cross-AZ numbers separately. For apples-to-apples, you want to compare the same network topology. We'll provide a small script to sample RTT and TLS handshake times continuously during the run.

[04:05] Priya Nair: Can you outline the exact steps for an apples-to-apples comparison? We want to present results to execs and they'd expect reproducibility.

[04:12] Mateo Ruiz: Sure, canonical steps:
- Fix model artifact and tokenizer (same commit hash).
- Use the same sequence length cap and truncation policy.
- Use identical prompt set and random seeds for any stochastic sampling.
- Warmup KV cache with the same policy and record pre/post hit-rates.
- Run multiple iterations with cold-starts and steady-state windows; report medians and confidence intervals.
- Report hardware details (GPU model, driver, CUDA/cuDNN/compilers) and runtime kernel versions.
- When testing quantization, run a regression matrix against prompt buckets and include qualitative checks (headlines, instruction following).

[05:05] Priya Nair: Great. about reproducibility: how do you handle non-determinism from async batching?

[05:13] Mateo Ruiz: You should control batching parameters: max batch size, max latency, and batching window. Fix them across tests. For added determinism, we run under a pinned runtime build and disable heuristics that dynamically alter the batch window. There's still some timing jitter but it's small if you report p95/p99 and run sufficient samples.

[05:40] Speaker 2: (inaudible) also note that some runtimes expose a "deterministic mode" which reduces throughput a bit but stabilizes latency.

[05:52] Omar Haddad: About tooling — what do you provide vs we build?

[05:56] Ava Chen: We have a benchmark harness that uses Locust for arrival patterns and a small runner that talks to the Redwood API or Dedicated endpoints. We'll share configs for warmup, sampling, and how to collect KV cache metrics. You can run it in your VPC and it will emit Prometheus metrics to your sink, or we can run it from a Redwood-managed runner for initial experiments.

[06:18] Priya Nair: will we need to modify our prompts? some of our prompts include embedded metadata that inflates token counts, which might change cost comparisons between quantized and fp32 models.

[06:27] Mateo Ruiz: Good point. we recommend a normalization pass: strip non-essential metadata and ensure the prompt formatting is identical across runs. Also log raw token counts and effective tokenization so you can normalize cost per semantic token.

[06:45] Sinead O'Connor: On auditability — if we run workload in a private cluster, can we still get per-request text payloads for debugging? compliance might want redaction controls.

[06:57] Ava Chen: Yes — we can include per-request payloads in the debug sink with automatic PII redaction rules. For compliance we support configurable retention windows and rotate keys via your KMS. We'll send the exact retention and redaction options in our follow-up.

[07:15] Priya Nair: Let's talk metrics we should surface in the deliverable.

[07:20] Mateo Ruiz: Minimal set: p50/p95/p99 latency (inference-only and end-to-end), token throughput (tokens/sec), KV cache hit-rate, batch size distribution over time, CPU/GPU utilization, memory pressure, and qualitative quality regression scores per prompt bucket. Also include a cost model: $/1M tokens given batching & quantization settings.

[07:52] Omar Haddad: about batch-size distribution — how do you capture the dynamic batches?

[07:58] Mateo Ruiz: The runtime emits batch-size histograms per second; our harness scrapes these and computes time-weighted averages. We also capture queueing latency inside the batching window. Those two together explain p50 vs p95 differences.

[08:20] Speaker 3 (Priya): We've seen weird behavior where quantized models increase average batch size but also increase p95 — any idea why?

[08:29] Mateo Ruiz: Could be because quantized runtimes are faster per-token so they drain faster, changing the shape of batching windows and causing more early small batches under spikey traffic. That can increase variance; it's another reason to test under representative arrival patterns.

[08:48] Priya Nair: What's the expected speedup ranges for 4-bit vs 8-bit on say a T4 or A10?

[08:56] Mateo Ruiz: Rough numbers: int8 might get you 1.2-1.6x token throughput; int4 can be 1.8-2.5x depending on kernel support and sequence length. But quality impacts vary; for some instruction-heavy prompts 4-bit can cause regressions. We'll provide profile charts from previous runs.

[09:20] Sinead O'Connor: any gotchas for on-prem GPUs — driver mismatches, MIG, etc?

[09:26] Mateo Ruiz: Yes: driver/CUDA mismatches, NVidia driver versions, MIG partitioning differences, and NIC firmware can all change perf. Also ensure hugepages and IO scheduler settings are consistent. For reproducibility, capture the full system info as a metadata artifact.

[09:45] Omar Haddad: For VPC setups, you mentioned we can run a node in our VPC. how does autoscaling work for Dedicated?

[09:53] Ava Chen: Dedicated supports pool autoscaling with configurable headroom and burst capacity. For the pilot we recommend a fixed pool to reduce variability, then test scaling behavior in a separate run.

[10:10] Priya Nair: can we fold in A/B quality checks automatically as part of the harness? like human judgments or automated SAMPLex checks?

[10:20] Mateo Ruiz: We support automated quality checks: BLEU/ROUGE/EM for structured outputs and embedding similarity for semantic checks. For human evals we can export blind buckets and integrate with user study tools. We also include hallucination detectors for common failure modes.

[10:38] Ava Chen: quick recap before we split: we'll send the harness, quant profiles, SOC2 docs, and an initial pilot plan. Pilot target: run the same harness against your Dedicated VPC and against a Redwood-hosted configuration, compare p50/p95 and quality across prompt buckets.

[10:58] Priya Nair: timeline is tight — we want results for the exec review on June 15. is that feasible?

[11:06] Ava Chen: Yes, if we get the trace and prompts by May 27 we can run the pilot and deliver results by June 12, giving you time to prep for the exec.

[11:20] Omar Haddad: ok, last question — how do you handle cost normalization across GPUs? we might test A10 vs A100.

[11:28] Mateo Ruiz: Normalize by effective tokens/sec and then compute $/token using current hourly GPU prices or your internal cost model. Report both raw perf and normalized cost. Also include amortized setup costs for dedicated pools.

[11:45] (cross talk)

[11:52] Sinead O'Connor: thanks, that was helpful — looking forward to the docs.

[11:58] Ava Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the repo link and the pilot plan.

[12:05] (meeting ends)

Notes: transcription includes some minor recognition errors (e.g., "K V cache", "quantize" vs "quant"). Attachments mentioned: benchmark-template.md, harness repo link (shared privately post-call), SOC2 packet.
